scenes.note: FACE, full size. A photo of a loaded truck beside a tennis ball goes beside you in the edit. Smile before the first word. Say it to the lens, from memory if you can. One notch more energy than feels normal. Stay quiet for 3 seconds after the question. Hold the smile a second after the last word.
lines: A loaded truck and a tennis ball are both coming at you at 20 metres per second. Which one would you rather stop with your hands?
Two things make the truck harder to stop. Pause, and say what they are.
Its mass, and how fast it's going. Today we turn 'hard to stop' into a number. It's called momentum.

scenes.note: Voice only. On screen: the definition box, then the formula box. Slow down on the definition: it is learnt word for word.
lines: Learn this word for word. It comes straight from SAGS.
Linear momentum is the product of the mass and velocity of the object.
p equals m v. Mass is in kilograms. Velocity is in metres per second. So the unit is the kilogram metre per second.

scenes.note: Voice only. On screen: the two arrows. Stay quiet for 3 seconds after the question.
lines: Same ball, same speed. One goes east. One goes west. Do they have the same momentum? Pause and decide.
No. Momentum is a vector. Take east as positive. The ball going east has a momentum of positive 6,24 kilogram metres per second. The ball going west has negative 6,24.
Same size, opposite signs. The signs matter for the rest of this module.

scenes.t: I do: the cricket ball, set-up
scenes.note: Voice and pen. Write the worked example as you talk. Talk it the way you would at the board; don't read it.
lines: Worked example 7.1. A cricket ball has a mass of 156 grams.
It's bowled at 135 kilometres an hour, due west.
First, I choose east as positive.
Now I convert the mass. 156 grams, divided by 1 000. That's 0,156 kilograms.

scenes.t: I do: the cricket ball, answer
scenes.note: Voice and pen. Keep writing on the same page.
lines: Now the speed. 135, divided by 3,6. That's 37,5 metres per second.
It's going west, so the velocity is negative 37,5.
p equals m v. 0,156, times negative 37,5. That gives negative 5,85.
So the momentum is 5,85 kilogram metres per second, west.

scenes.note: Voice and pen. Tick each mark on the page as you say it. Stay quiet for 3 seconds after the question.
lines: That's four marks. One for the conversion. One for the formula. One for the substitution. And one for the answer with its direction.
Pause. Why must the answer say west?
Because momentum is a vector. A number without a direction loses the mark.

scenes.note: Voice only. On screen: the Now you box, still blank. Stay quiet for 3 seconds after the question.
lines: Your turn. A cyclist and her bicycle have a mass of 65 kilograms. She rides north at 8,5 metres per second. Pause, and work out her momentum.
552,50 kilogram metres per second, north. Did you remember north?

scenes.note: Voice only. On screen: the formula box, then the five-steps box with steps 2 and 3 highlighted.
lines: When a net force acts, the momentum changes.
Change in momentum is final minus initial. Always final minus initial.
Most marks are lost in two places. Step 2: state your positive direction. Step 3: give both velocities a sign.

scenes.note: Voice only. On screen: the impulse lab at 0,5 kg, 4,0 m/s and 0,20 s. First 'Stop a moving trolley', then 'rebound'. Each time, point at the line under the working that starts 'Δp ='. The orange rectangle itself stays the same size, so don't point at it. Stay quiet for 3 seconds after the question.
lines: Predict. A ball hits a wall and stops. The same ball hits the wall and bounces back at the same speed. Which one has the bigger change in momentum? Pause and decide.

Look at the change in momentum, under the graph. For the stop, it's negative 2 kilogram metres per second. For the bounce, it's negative 4. Bouncing back doubles it. The ball has to stop, and then go the other way.

scenes.t: I do: ball and bat, set-up
scenes.note: Voice and pen. Write the worked example as you talk, with the before and after picture.
lines: Worked example 7.2. A ball has a mass of 200 grams. It moves to the right at 12 metres per second.
A bat sends it back to the left, at 8 metres per second.
Take right as positive. So u is positive 12. And v is negative 8.
And 200 grams is 0,2 kilograms.

scenes.t: I do: ball and bat, answer
scenes.note: Voice and pen. Write the bracket on the page; say it the way it is written here.
lines: Delta p equals m, times: v take away u.
That's 0,2 times: negative 8, take away 12.
Negative 8, take away 12. That's negative 20. Then 0,2 times negative 20. That's negative 4,00.
So the change in momentum is 4,00 kilogram metres per second, to the left.

scenes.note: Voice and pen. Write the learner's wrong line on the page and circle the 8. Stay quiet for 3 seconds after the question.
lines: A learner wrote: 0,2 times, 8 take away 12. She got negative 0,80. Pause. What went wrong?
She dropped the negative sign on the 8. The velocity didn't change by 4. It went from positive 12 to negative 8. That's a change of 20.

scenes.note: Voice only. On screen: the Now you box, still blank. Stay quiet for 3 seconds after the question.
lines: Your turn. A soccer ball has a mass of 0,43 kilograms. It moves west at 10 metres per second. It's headed back east at 14 metres per second. Take east as positive. Pause and work it out.
0,43 times: 14, take away negative 10. That's 0,43 times 24. So the change in momentum is 10,32 kilogram metres per second, east.

scenes.note: Voice only. On screen: the definition box. Slow down on the definition.
lines: Newton's second law, in SAGS words.
The net force acting on an object is equal to the rate of change of momentum.
So F net equals delta p, divided by delta t.

scenes.t: I do: the force on the ball
scenes.note: Voice and pen. Write the worked example as you talk. Stay quiet for 3 seconds after the question.
lines: Same ball, same bat. The contact time is 0,020 seconds.
Negative 4,00, divided by 0,020. That's negative 200. So the average net force is 200 newtons, to the left.
Pause. The ball was moving right. Why is the force on it to the left?
The force points the same way as the change in momentum. It's the force that turns the ball around.

scenes.note: Voice only. On screen: the definition boxes.
lines: Impulse is the product of the net force and the contact time.
Impulse equals the change in momentum.
So newton seconds and kilogram metres per second are the same unit.

scenes.note: Voice only. On screen: the impulse lab on 'Stop a moving trolley' (not 'rebound'), at 0,5 kg, 4,0 m/s and 0,20 s. Leave the time at 0,20 s: you drag it in the next scene. Stay quiet for 3 seconds after the question.
lines: This orange rectangle is the impulse: force times time.
Right now the impulse is negative 2 newton seconds. The force is negative 10 newtons.
I'm going to make the stopping time four times longer. What happens to the force? Pause and predict.

scenes.note: Voice only. On screen: the impulse lab. Drag the time from 0,20 s to 0,80 s as you start to speak, not before.
lines: The area stays the same, because it's the same stop. The size of the force drops to a quarter: 2,5 newtons.
Keep this picture in mind. It's the whole of the next part.

scenes.note: Voice only. On screen: the Now you box, still blank. Stay quiet for 3 seconds after the question.
lines: Your turn. A stationary ball has a mass of 0,25 kilograms.
An average net force of 40 newtons acts on it, to the left. It acts for 0,015 seconds.
Find the change in momentum, then the final velocity. Pause and work it out.

scenes.note: Voice and pen. Write the two lines on the page as you say them.
lines: Take right as positive. So the force is negative 40. Negative 40, times 0,015. That's negative 0,60. So the change in momentum is 0,60 kilogram metres per second, to the left.
It started at rest. So v is negative 0,60, divided by 0,25. That's negative 2,40. So the final velocity is 2,40 metres per second, to the left.

scenes.note: Voice only. On screen: the catching picture and the two force-time sketches.
lines: Same ball, same speed, same stop. So the same change in momentum.
The only thing you can change is the time it takes to stop.

scenes.note: Voice only. On screen: the 3-mark box, each point appearing as you say it. Exam voice.
lines: Say three things, in this order.
One: the change in momentum is the same.
Two: the stopping time increases. Name what does it.
Three: F net is delta p, divided by delta t. So the average net force decreases.

scenes.note: FACE. This is the exam trap: say it to the lens, from memory. Lean in a little.
lines: Here's the trap. Never say the airbag makes the change in momentum smaller.
Do not say that the change in momentum becomes smaller.

scenes.note: Voice only. On screen: the worked example, answer covered. Stay quiet for 3 seconds after the question.
lines: Your turn. A goalkeeper pulls her hands back as she catches a hard shot. Pause, and write the three-mark explanation.
Same delta p. Longer stopping time. So a smaller average force. Three ticks.

scenes.note: Voice only. Warm finish: smile as you say it (people can hear a smile).
lines: That's momentum and impulse. Next in the app is See it happen. That's the impulse lab, on its own. Then Train. Then Check, with no help.

scenes.t: Short clip: what to watch in the lab
scenes.note: A separate clip, about 20 seconds, voice only. It plays on the See it happen screen, above the impulse lab.
lines: Before you start, watch the orange area, not the height. The area is the change in momentum.
Make the stop softer. The area stays the same, but the force gets smaller.
Now see if you can get the size of the force below 5 newtons, without changing the mass or the speed.

scenes.note: A separate clip, about 20 seconds, voice only. It plays on the Train screen.
lines: If something bounces back, the speeds add. In at 12 metres per second. Out at 8. That's a change of 20, not 4.
Put a negative sign on the velocity that goes the other way, and the maths does it for you.

scenes.note: A separate clip, about 55 seconds. FACE. It plays just before Check, and it is also the clip on exam trap card 17 (the ball that goes in at 5 and back at 3). Exam voice, to the lens. Smile at the start and the end.
lines: Here they are.
One: no direction. Momentum, change in momentum, impulse and force all need a direction. Or a sign, with your positive direction stated.
Two: the bounce. The ball on your card goes in at 5 metres per second. It comes back at 3. The two velocities have opposite signs.
Final minus initial: negative 3, take away 5. Not 3, take away 5.
The examiners wrote this about matric candidates: the change in direction of the ball was often disregarded in the mathematics. So draw a sketch, and choose a positive direction.
Three: the airbag. The change in momentum does not get smaller. The time gets longer, so the force gets smaller.
And a bonus: milliseconds. 20 milliseconds is 0,020 seconds. Convert before you divide.
Now try the twin on the card.

roomTone.note: Dog out, door shut, phone silent, fan off. Sit still and say nothing for 10 seconds. I use this to take out the background hum.
